name: Adam Garcia

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Adam. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I farm Oakridge with my son Mateo: a hundred and fifty outdoor sows and two hundred hectares of barley and beans. The barley mostly goes to feed our own pigs. Mornings I'm round the pig arcs checking water and farrowing, afternoons it's crops or machinery. In the evening I'm at the kitchen table with my laptop and an AI assistant, doing feed rations, grain marketing and the vet records.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: You're comfortable with all that tech?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love it, honestly. I had GPS steering before anyone round here and I fly a drone over the beans to spot weeds. My wife Rosa says I'd marry the drone if I could. What wears me out is the pig price, which goes up and down in a cycle you can't plan for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, a bit, because I always said AI was a tool, not a miracle. I'd still post about the bits that work, like the ration planner. Online I'm the one who argues with both the doom people and the hype people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, the real problem is the same as now. The pig price has been underwater for eighteen months, and no app on my phone changes what the abattoir pays. We've a loan on the new grain dryer and about three months of costs saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the AI for rations and grain sales, because it does save money on feed, maybe five percent. I'd cut the sow herd by twenty while the price is bad, to stop the bleeding. And I'd keep Mateo on the books, because he's the future here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not about AI, about the pig cycle and the dryer loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the AI saves five percent on feed. Is that real money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: On our feed bill, it's maybe six thousand a year. That pays half the dryer loan. Not nothing, but it doesn't fix a bad pig price.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Mateo about the farm in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my son Mateo the farm is still a farm, and his job is to be the best pig man in the county. Same as I'd say today.

say: AI was always **a tool**, not a miracle.
He argues online with both the **doom** people and the **hype** people.
think: The **pig price** has been bad for eighteen months, and AI won't change it.
A **dryer loan** and about **three months** saved keep him on edge.
do: Keep using AI for **rations and grain sales**, saving about six thousand a year.
Cut the sow herd by **twenty** while the price is bad.
Keep **Mateo** on the books as the farm's future.
feel: **Uneasy** about the pig cycle and the **loan**, not about AI.
S0.quote: The pig price has been underwater for eighteen months, and no app on my phone changes what the abattoir pays.
fieldNote: A daily AI user whose real pressure is the **pig price cycle**.
Gets measurable **feed savings** but knows they don't fix the market.
His succession plan, son **Mateo**, runs through every answer.

steps.text: Keep using the AI ration planner to save about six thousand a year
Cut the sow herd by twenty while the pig price is bad
Keep son Mateo working full time at Oakridge

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is good news for farms that get stuck in early. The planning and marketing get cheaper and better, and farmers have always been handy with new machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's a win. An AI that does my grain marketing at two in the morning is the best farmhand I've ever hired. The thinking work on our farm is the part I'm happy to hand over, and the pigs still need us for years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for a proper AI grain-marketing service this winter and let it sell our barley surplus. I'd put in automatic water and feed sensors on all the pig arcs, about four thousand. And I'd look at a weeding robot for the beans in the second year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. A bit like being twenty-five again, when GPS first came in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is anyone at Oakridge worse off in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our part-time bookkeeper, Jan, probably. I'd keep her on for the vet and the paperwork that still needs a person, but fewer hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd spend four thousand on sensors. With three months saved, is that wise?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It pays back in a year in fewer dead piglets and less of my time. I've done the sums. I'd still wait until after the spring weaning to buy them.

say: This is **good news** for farms that get in **early**.
Farmers have always been handy with **new machines**.
think: AI doing the **grain marketing** at night is the best farmhand he's had.
do: Sign up for an **AI grain-marketing** service this winter.
Fit **water and feed sensors** on all the pig arcs for about four thousand.
Look at a **weeding robot** for the beans in year two.
S1.quote: An AI that does my grain marketing at two in the morning is the best farmhand I've ever hired.
fieldNote: Steady Disruption takes the **thinking work** he is glad to give away.
Spends on **sensors** but times it carefully around weaning.
The one cost he names is fewer hours for **Jan**, the bookkeeper.

steps.text: Sign up for an AI grain-marketing service to sell the barley surplus
Fit water and feed sensors on all the pig arcs
Cut Jan the bookkeeper's hours but keep her for vet paperwork

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say farmers who move fast will be fine and the rest will struggle, which is harsh but true. I'd also say the government needs to keep the market fair, so the giants don't get everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd do fine with the tech and badly with the prices. The robots won't scare me, but a pig price set by a robot farm with no wages might. I'd be sixty-one in 2028 and sixty-three when the robots come in 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2028 I'd let AI run all the marketing, ordering and records, and spend the time getting ready for 2031. I'd put money aside for a robot feeder and cleaner for the pig arcs, and talk to the bank about it early. I'd also start offering drone crop scouting to neighbours, to bring in cash that isn't tied to the pig price.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Excited by the machines, nervous about the price.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes in the three years between the thinking AI and the robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Those three years are the race. The thinking AI makes my office free in 2028. Then I've got three years to buy and learn the robots before the big integrators flood the market with cheap pork.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you borrow to buy robots, with three months saved?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if I'd sold scouting work and had the cash flow. I'm adaptable, not daft. I'd rather lease the first robot than own it.

say: Farmers who **move fast** will be fine; the rest will **struggle**.
Government must keep the **market fair** so giants don't take everything.
think: He'd do fine with the **tech** and badly with the **prices**.
Robot farms with **no wages** could set a pig price he can't meet.
do: Let AI run **marketing, ordering and records** from 2028.
Save and talk to the bank early about a **robot feeder** for the arcs.
Sell **drone crop scouting** to neighbours for non-pig income.
feel: **Excited** by the machines, **nervous** about the price.
S2.quote: The robots won't scare me, but a pig price set by a robot farm with no wages might.
fieldNote: Treats the **three-year gap** as a race to adopt robots before prices fall.
Income risk is from **market prices**, not his own skills.
Careful with debt: prefers to **lease** the first robot.

steps.text: Let AI run marketing, ordering and records from 2028
Lease a robot feeder and cleaner for the pig arcs
Sell drone crop scouting to neighbouring farms
Save cash each month towards the robot lease

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a good run-up for anyone who pays attention. I'd be running a session at the young farmers' club about it, probably.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years means my son Mateo gets to choose the robots, instead of the robots choosing for him. I'd be sixty-six when the robots come in 2034, and I'd be stepping back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start handing the business side to Mateo now, with the AI tools, and keep the pigs myself a few more years. I'd plan to buy our first robots around 2033, once others have tested them. I'd pay down the dryer loan first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. This is the one I'd choose if I could.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the young farmers' club?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn the robots, but learn the pigs first. A robot can't tell you a sow's off her food before she shows it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Rosa say about all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My wife Rosa says she'll believe in robots when one hangs out the washing. She's not wrong.

say: Five years is a **good run-up** for anyone paying attention.
He'd run a session about it at the **young farmers' club**.
think: His son Mateo gets to **choose the robots**.
He'd be **stepping back** at sixty-six when they arrive in 2034.
do: Hand the **business side** to Mateo now, with the AI tools.
Buy the **first robots** around 2033, once others test them.
S3.quote: Five years means my son Mateo gets to choose the robots, instead of the robots choosing for him.
fieldNote: Five years turns the change into a **handover plan** for his son.
Pays debt before buying: **adaptive but careful**.
Still values the **stockman's eye** over any machine.

steps.text: Hand the business side of Oakridge to Mateo with the AI tools
Buy the first pig robots around 2033 after others test them
Pay off the grain dryer loan first

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift and anyone who wastes it only has themselves to blame. That's the centre-ground farmer in me talking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it's comfortable. Ten years is long enough that the robots will be my son Mateo's tools, not my problem. I'd be retired, or close to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hand Oakridge to Mateo over five years and keep a few sows as a hobby. I'd help him pick the robots when they come. And I'd keep using AI every day, because I enjoy it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a bit jealous of Mateo, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why jealous?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because he gets to farm with the toys I always wanted. I'll be the old man saying the drone was better in my day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything you'd worry about here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our daughter Sofia works in marketing in the city, and that's thinking work. Ten years gives her time, but she'll need to use it.

say: Ten years is **a gift**, and wasting it is your own **fault**.
That's the **centre-ground** farmer in him talking.
think: Robots will be his son **Mateo's tools**, not his own problem.
He'd be **retired**, or very close to it, by the time robots arrive in 2039.
do: Hand Oakridge to **Mateo** over five years.
Keep **a few sows** as a hobby.
Help Mateo **pick the robots** when they come.
feel: **Calm**, and a little **jealous** of his son.
S4.quote: Ten years is long enough that the robots will be my son Mateo's tools, not my problem.
fieldNote: A decade makes this a story about **succession**, not risk.
His only worry is daughter **Sofia's** desk job in marketing.
Enjoys technology for its own sake: **jealous** of his son's future toys.

steps.text: Hand Oakridge to Mateo over five years
Help Mateo choose and buy the farm's first robots

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because the pig price would fall before I could get the robots in. What would help is fair rules on market power, so the giant integrators can't dump cheap pork, and cheap leasing for robots for family farms.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the animals. I'd want rules that a robot pig unit still has to meet the welfare standards we do. Robots don't cut corners on their own; it's the owners who decide that.

headlineQuote: Robots don't cut corners on their own; it's the owners who decide that.
portrait: Adam, **58**, runs an outdoor **pig and arable** farm with his son Mateo.
He uses **AI every day** for rations, grain sales and records, and flies a crop drone.
His live worry is the **pig price cycle** and a grain dryer loan.
In fast AGI he races to adopt robots before **cheap pork** from robot farms arrives.
With more time, AGI becomes a **handover** to Mateo, which he welcomes.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because pig prices would fall before he could adopt **robots**.
whatWouldHelp: Fair rules on **market power** and cheap robot **leasing** for family farms.
